title: Rococo
objective: After this level you can describe the playful, pastel Rococo style.
summary: Rococo began in early-1700s Paris as a lighter answer to Louis XIV's heavy Baroque: shell-like curves, pastels and flirtation. Fragonard's The Swing, with its flying slipper, is its signature.

cards.headline: A pink dress, a swing, and a slipper flying through the air.
cards.body: In Fragonard's The Swing (about 1767 to 1768), a young woman flies up in pink silk. An older man pushes the swing. Down in the bushes, a young lover gazes up. One of her slippers has just kicked off into the air. Welcome to the Rococo.

cards.headline: From grand to cozy
cards.body: Rococo began in Paris in the early 1700s as a reaction against the heavy Baroque of Louis XIV's reign. Think of a switch from a cathedral organ to a harpsichord. It flourished from about 1700 to 1770, filling paintings with myth and courtship instead of saints and struggle.

cards.fact: Rococo is named after grotto seashells.
cards.context: The word comes from the French rocaille, the shell-covered rockwork used to decorate artificial grottoes. The style loved curling C and S shapes, light pastels, ivory white and gold, and lighthearted scenes of myth and courtship. If Baroque shouts, Rococo flirts.

mascot.line: Easy to mix up. Baroque: the lumpy pearl. Rococo: the grotto seashells.

cards.headline: The Swing's cheeky backstory
cards.body: According to an account from 1767, a gentleman of the court first asked the painter Doyen for a picture of his mistress on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself admiring her legs. Doyen refused and passed the job to Fragonard. By then, critics were already attacking Rococo as frivolous, and a stricter style would soon replace it in France.
